title: Martin de Porres
hookLine: a mixed-race Dominican brother in Lima who cared for the sick, poor and animals

lines: A DOG, A CAT, A MOUSE.
cards: A broom. Not a crown, not a book, not a sword. In paintings and statues of one saint from Peru, that's what he holds: a plain broom, the kind in any closet.
Sometimes there's a dog, a cat and a mouse at his feet, eating from the same dish.
The law of his day kept him at the bottom of the ladder, the son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Black mother, and he spent his life at the jobs nobody wanted.

teach.b: Martin de Porres was born in Lima, in colonial Peru. His Spanish father was slow to acknowledge him. His mother had been enslaved and was freed.
As a boy Martin was apprenticed to a barber-surgeon, which then meant cutting hair, setting bones, bleeding fevers and mixing herbs. Then he knocked at the door of the Dominican friars.
Because of his race, the rules of the time didn't allow him to enter as a full member.
So he came in as a helper, doing the lowest work in the house: sweeping, laundry, caring for the sick. Only later was he allowed to make vows as a lay brother. He never stopped sweeping.

That's our line: the broom saint. Martin ran the friary's infirmary and treated the sick of the city too, rich and poor, Spanish, African and indigenous. He begged for food and money for those who had none.
Stories gathered around him: healings, being in two places at once, animals.
One tells how mice were raiding the friary, and instead of poisoning them, Martin led them out to the garden and promised to feed them there if they'd stay out of the linen.
Another tells that when the friary fell into debt, he offered to be sold as a slave to pay it. Whether every story happened as told, they show what people saw in him.

His life reads like Jesus's words in Matthew: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." And the psalm: "his tender mercies are over all his works."
All his works, including the mice. The Catholic Church honors Martin as a saint.

how: Catholics in Peru and beyond keep the feast of Saint Martin de Porres, and he is pictured with a broom; some parishes and charities named for him care for the sick, the poor or animals.

practice: If there's an animal near you, a pet, a bird at the window, even an ant on the floor, watch it closely and notice what it needs; if not, remember one you've known.
If you pray, give thanks for it with the psalm's words, his tender mercies are over all his works; if you don't, simply be kind.
